entities.summary: El Teniente is the world's largest underground copper mine, located in the Andes Mountains of central Chile at an elevation of 2,300 metres (7,500 ft) above sea level. It is operated by the state-owned mining company Codelco and constitutes the largest division of its operations. Mining at the site dates back to at least 1819, but large-scale industrial extraction began in 1906 under U.S. ownership, initially through the Braden Copper Company and later Kennecott Copper Corporation. In 1971, during the presidency of Salvador Allende, Chile nationalized its copper industry and acquired full ownership of El Teniente.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: El Teniente's large-scale industrial extraction began in 1906 under U.S. ownership, contributing to Chile's economic growth and establishing it as a major copper producer. The mine's nationalization in 1971 during the presidency of Salvador Allende marked a significant shift in Chile's industrial policies.
